en.name: Our Lady of Good Health
en.summary: Traditional sixteenth and seventeenth-century apparitions in a Tamil Nadu fishing village, now one of the most visited Marian shrines in Asia.
en.body: According to long-standing local tradition, the Virgin Mary appeared twice near the fishing village of Velankanni on India's southeastern coast: first to a young shepherd boy carrying milk for a customer, who reported meeting a beautiful lady holding a child who asked him for milk for her son, and again some years later to a crippled buttermilk vendor, whom Mary reportedly asked to build a chapel at the site before his health was restored. A separate and better-documented tradition holds that Portuguese sailors caught in a violent storm off the coast vowed to build a church in Mary's honor if they survived, and, having washed ashore safely near Velankanni on the feast of Our Lady's Nativity, fulfilled their vow, contributing to the shrine's early growth. Pope John XXIII raised the church to the status of a minor basilica in 1962, and the site, sometimes called the "Lourdes of the East," now draws millions of pilgrims of multiple faiths annually. In August 2024, the Vatican's Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith granted the shrine a Nihil obstat, the most favorable ruling available under Pope Francis's revised norms for discerning reported supernatural phenomena, permitting continued devotion without pronouncing definitively on the historical apparitions themselves.
